title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
learningObjective: Determine the inverse sine, cosine, and tangent values; graph inverse trigonometric functions and determine the limitations on the domain and range.

faqs.question: Why do we need inverse trig functions, and why can't we just invert sine, cosine, and tangent directly?
faqs.answer: Inverting a function requires it to be one-to-one (FN6) — but sine, cosine, and tangent are each far from one-to-one over their full domain, since infinitely many angles share the exact same sine, cosine, or tangent value. For example, \( \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \) and \( \cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right) \) are both \( \dfrac{1}{2} \) — so "the angle whose cosine is 1/2" can't have one honest answer unless we agree to restrict which angles we're allowed to pick from.

faqs.question: What is arcsine, and what domain restriction defines it?
faqs.answer:
Arcsine, written \( \arcsin(x) \), is the inverse of sine restricted to the domain \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \) — a stretch of the sine curve, centered at 0, where sine is one-to-one and hits every output from −1 to 1 exactly once. Other stretches would also work, but this is the one everyone agrees to use. \( \arcsin(x) \) is the unique angle \( \theta \) in that restricted interval such that \( \sin(\theta)=x \).

Only the thick, solid middle piece of sine, from x = −π/2 to x = π/2, is used to define arcsine. On that piece sine is one-to-one. The rest of the wave is dashed.

faqs.question: What is arccosine, and what domain restriction defines it?
faqs.answer: Arccosine, written \( \arccos(x) \), is the inverse of cosine restricted to the domain \( [0,\pi] \) — the interval where cosine steadily decreases from 1 down to −1 without ever repeating a value. \( \arccos(x) \) is the unique angle \( \theta \) in that restricted interval such that \( \cos(\theta)=x \).

faqs.question: What is arctangent, and why is its domain restriction an open interval instead of closed?
faqs.answer: Arctangent, written \( \arctan(x) \), is the inverse of tangent restricted to \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \) — using parentheses rather than brackets, because tangent itself is undefined at \( \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) (PF2's vertical asymptotes). Since those endpoints were never part of tangent's domain to begin with, they can't be included in arctangent's restriction either. That open interval is also the range of arctangent, so its graph levels off toward \( y=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) without reaching them.

faqs.question: Why doesn't sin⁻¹(x) mean the same thing as (sin(x))⁻¹?
faqs.answer: This notation is genuinely ambiguous at first glance, and it's worth being deliberate about it. \( \sin^{-1}(x) \) is just shorthand — commonly used on calculators — for \( \arcsin(x) \), the inverse function. It does not mean "raise sin(x) to the power −1," which would actually be \( \dfrac{1}{\sin(x)}=\csc(x) \) instead. (Compare \( \sin^2(x) \), which does mean \( (\sin(x))^2 \). That is exactly why \( \sin^{-1} \) is confusing.) Whenever there's doubt, writing \( \arcsin(x) \) instead of \( \sin^{-1}(x) \) avoids the confusion entirely.

faqs.question: How do I evaluate an inverse trig function like arcsin or arccos at a special value (like 1/2 or −√3/2), without a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Ask yourself: "what angle, within the correct restricted interval, has this value as its sine (or cosine, or tangent)?" Use your TR4/TR5 special-angle knowledge to recall which angle produces that value, then double check it actually falls within the required restricted range. Give the answer as an exact angle in radians, like \( -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \), not in degrees or as a decimal. That is the form CheckIt expects.
Worked Example

\( \arcsin\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \): which angle in \( \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right] \) has sine \( -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \)?

\( \arcsin\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \)

faqs.question: How do I evaluate an inverse trig function using a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Use the \( \sin^{-1} \), \( \cos^{-1} \), or \( \tan^{-1} \) button (usually accessed via a SHIFT or 2nd function key above the regular sin/cos/tan buttons). Make sure your calculator's angle mode (degrees or radians) matches what the problem is asking for before you evaluate.
Worked Example

\( \arccos\left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right) \approx 126.9° \) or \( \approx 2.21 \) radians

Extension: calculator values go beyond the PF3 CheckIt exercise, which asks for exact angles in radians at special values, with no calculator. If you use a calculator to check, set it to radians.

faqs.question: What is the domain and range of arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent?
faqs.answer:
Each inverse function's domain is the range of the restricted trig function, and its range is the restricted domain that was chosen.
Summary

\( \arcsin(x) \): domain \( [-1,1] \), range \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \)

\( \arccos(x) \): domain \( [-1,1] \), range \( [0,\pi] \)

\( \arctan(x) \): domain \( (-\infty,\infty) \), range \( \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \)

faqs.question: How do I graph arcsine, arccosine, or arctangent?
faqs.answer:
Each inverse trig graph is the mirror image, across the line \( y=x \), of the restricted piece of its original trig function (the same mirror-image idea you saw for logarithms and exponentials in EL4) — so the fastest way to sketch it is to take a few known points from the restricted original function and swap the x- and y-coordinates.

Only arcsine is drawn here: it exists only from x = −1 to x = 1, includes both endpoints, (−1, −π/2) and (1, π/2), and has range [−π/2, π/2]. The arccosine and arctangent graphs are in the guided-path stop "Graph and state domain and range."

faqs.question: How do I evaluate a composition like sin(arccos(5/13)) exactly, without a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Extension: compositions like this go beyond the PF3 CheckIt exercise. Let \( \theta=\arccos\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right) \), draw a right triangle with angle \( \theta \) where the adjacent side is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13, use the Pythagorean theorem to find the missing side, then read off whichever trig ratio the outer function is asking for.

Adjacent = 5, hypotenuse = 13, so the missing side (opposite) = 12 — giving sin(θ) = 12/13.

Worked Example

Missing side: \( \sqrt{13^2-5^2}=\sqrt{144}=12 \)

\( \sin\left(\arccos\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right)\right)=\sin(\theta)=\dfrac{12}{13} \)

faqs.question: How do I know which right triangle to draw when evaluating a composition of a trig function and an inverse trig function?
faqs.answer: Extension: the triangle method goes beyond the PF3 CheckIt exercise. Look at what's inside the inverse trig function — that fraction tells you the ratio of two sides, so you can use its numerator and denominator as those two side lengths. If it's \( \arcsin\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) \), the opposite side is \( a \) and the hypotenuse is \( b \) (since sine is opposite/hypotenuse). If it's \( \arccos\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) \), the adjacent side is \( a \) and the hypotenuse is \( b \). If it's \( \arctan\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) \), the opposite side is \( a \) and the adjacent side is \( b \). Whichever two sides you're given, the Pythagorean theorem finds the third. This works directly when the input is positive. If the input is negative, the angle is not in Quadrant I: use the range of the inverse function to decide the sign of your answer. For example, \( \tan\left(\arcsin\left(-\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\right) = -\dfrac{3}{4} \), because that angle is in Quadrant IV.

faqs.question: How do I evaluate a composition like cos(arcsin(x)) that has a variable instead of a number?
faqs.answer:
Extension: compositions with a variable go beyond the PF3 CheckIt exercise. Name the inner angle, use the Pythagorean identity, then let the range of the inverse function decide the sign. This works for every allowed \( x \), including negative values and the ends of the domain.
Worked Example

Find \( \cos(\arcsin(x)) \). Let \( \theta=\arcsin(x) \), so \( \sin(\theta)=x \), with \( x \) in \( [-1,1] \).

From \( \sin^2(\theta)+\cos^2(\theta)=1 \): \( \cos^2(\theta)=1-x^2 \), so \( \cos(\theta)=\pm\sqrt{1-x^2} \).

Since \( \theta \) is in \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \), \( \cos(\theta) \) is nonnegative, so take the nonnegative root.

\( \cos(\arcsin(x)) = \sqrt{1-x^2} \), for \( -1\le x\le 1 \)

Picture check: when \( 0<x<1 \), you can draw the triangle from faq-10 and faq-11 with opposite side \( x \) and hypotenuse \( 1 \); the adjacent side is \( \sqrt{1-x^2} \), which matches. The identity is what covers negative \( x \) and the end values \( x=0 \) and \( x=\pm1 \), where no triangle can be drawn.

faqs.question: How does this section connect to FN6's inverse function ideas and TR5's exact trig values?
faqs.answer: This section is FN6's entire inverse-function framework — one-to-one requirement, domain restriction, domain/range swapping — applied specifically to sine, cosine, and tangent. And every "evaluate without a calculator" question here leans directly on TR5's reference-angle and exact-value work, just run in the opposite direction: instead of angle → trig value, you're going trig value → angle.

faqs.question: Why do inverse trig functions matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Any time you know a ratio (a slope, a height-to-distance ratio, a physical measurement) and need to find the actual angle that produced it — like finding the angle of a wheelchair ramp from its rise and run, or angles in navigation, physics, and engineering — you need an inverse trig function. They're also essential in calculus, where derivatives and integrals involving inverse trig functions show up often once you start working with more advanced techniques.

guided.title: Why Inverse Trig Needs a Restricted Domain
guided.prompt: I'm learning why sine, cosine, and tangent need restricted domains before they can have inverses. My notes say: arcsin gives angles in [-pi/2, pi/2], arccos gives angles in [0, pi], and arctan gives angles strictly between -pi/2 and pi/2. Start by asking me to list every angle from 0 to 2pi with cos(theta) = 1/2, and ask me: why would reversing these input-output pairs fail to define an inverse function? Don't explain anything until I've answered. Then ask me which of my angles arccos(1/2) has to be, and why. Next, write a 3- or 4-sentence explanation of why the restriction for cosine is [0, pi] instead of [-pi/2, pi/2], and include one deliberate mistake in it for me to find. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Grade a Classmate's Inverse Trig Values
guided.prompt: I'm practicing exact values of arcsin, arccos, and arctan for my PF3 CheckIt. My notes say: arcsin gives angles in [-pi/2, pi/2], arccos gives angles in [0, pi], arctan gives angles strictly between -pi/2 and pi/2, and answers are exact angles in radians. Pretend you're a classmate. Evaluate six expressions, two for each function, using only these inputs. For arcsin and arccos: 0, 1, -1, 1/2, -1/2, sqrt(2)/2, -sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2, -sqrt(3)/2. For arctan: 0, 1, -1, sqrt(3)/3, -sqrt(3)/3, sqrt(3), -sqrt(3). Include at least one input of 0, 1, or -1, and at least one negative input to arccos. Get two of the six wrong in realistic ways, like an angle outside the range or a negative arccos answer. Show only your final answers. I'll grade each one and use the range to explain every fix. Don't tell me which ones are wrong until I've graded all six. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Triangle Method for Compositions
guided.prompt: This goes beyond the PF3 CheckIt exercise. I'm learning to evaluate compositions like sin(arccos(5/13)) with a right triangle. Give me one composition with a positive fraction inside. Before you help, ask me which two sides of the triangle that fraction gives me, and why. Let me find the third side and the final ratio myself, and give a hint only when I ask. Then solve tan(arcsin(-3/5)) yourself, step by step, and make one deliberate mistake (for example, losing the sign or labeling the wrong sides). I'll find it and explain how the range of arcsin decides the sign. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Compositions with a Variable
guided.prompt: This goes beyond the PF3 CheckIt exercise. I'm learning to write compositions like cos(arcsin(x)) as expressions in x. My notes say: let theta = arcsin(x), use sin^2(theta) + cos^2(theta) = 1, then use the range of arcsin to decide the sign, so cos(arcsin(x)) = sqrt(1 - x^2) for -1 <= x <= 1. Ask me to find tan(arccos(x)) one step at a time, with hints only when I ask. Make me say which x values are allowed, how I know the sign, and what happens at x = 0. Then show me your own answer for sin(arctan(x)), including the x values it works for, with one deliberate mistake in it (for example, a wrong sign or a wrong domain). I'll find the mistake and test your answer by plugging in x = 1 and x = -1 and comparing with exact values I know. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Graph It by Swapping: Domain, Range, and Sketch
guided.prompt: I'm connecting inverse functions from FN6 to the graphs of arcsin, arccos, and arctan in PF3. My notes say an inverse swaps the coordinates of every point, so it swaps domain and range. Ask me to list three points on y = cos(x) for x from 0 to pi, swap them, and tell you the domain and range of y = arccos(x). Wait for my answer, and if I'm wrong, correct me with a question instead of the answer. Then describe, in words, a sketch of y = arctan(x): its domain, its range in interval notation, three points on it, and what happens at the far left and right. Put one deliberate mistake in your description (for example, square brackets on the range or a wrong point). I'll find it and check it against my notes. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

paths.label: PF3: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
paths.intro: Builds to the PF3 check: computing inverse sine, cosine, and tangent values, and graphing an inverse trig function with its domain and range. Practice scope: the path uses the special values from the PF3 CheckIt exercise (0, ±1, ±1/2, ±√2/2, ±√3/2, and for tangent ±√3/3 and ±√3), with exact answers in radians. The stop "Extension: Inverse of a value outside the range" is optional.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews PF3 leans on: exact values (TR5) and inverse functions (FN6). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Exact values on the unit circle
stops.target: Recall from TR5: exact values of \(\sin\), \(\cos\), and \(\tan\) at special angles, with the sign from the quadrant.
stops.coldPlain: Find sin(pi/6), cos(5pi/6), tan(pi/3), and sin(-pi/4).
stops.solution: pi/6: sin = 1/2. 5pi/6 is in QII with reference pi/6, so cos = -sqrt3/2. tan(pi/3) = (sqrt3/2)/(1/2) = sqrt3. -pi/4 is in QIV, so sin = -sqrt2/2.
stops.mistake: Dropping the sign for angles outside Quadrant I.
stops.again: Which angle in \(\left[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) has \(\cos\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)? Which has \(\tan\theta = 1\)?
stops.reflect: If \(\sin\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}\), how many angles \(\theta\) could you name? Which one would you pick as "the" answer, and why?

stops.title: Inverses need one-to-one
stops.target: Recall from FN6: a function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test). The inverse swaps domain and range: if \(f(a) = b\), then \(f^{-1}(b) = a\).
stops.cold: Does \(y = \sin x\) (for all real \(x\)) pass the horizontal line test? Use the line \(y = \tfrac{1}{2}\).
stops.coldPlain: Does y = sin x (for all real x) pass the horizontal line test? Use the line y = 1/2.
stops.coldA: No. \(y = \tfrac{1}{2}\) hits the full sine curve infinitely often (\(\tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}, \ldots\)). But the solid piece from \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) is hit only once.[[graph:RESTRICT]]
stops.solution: sin x = 1/2 at pi/6, 5pi/6, and at every angle 2pi more or less than those, so it is not one-to-one. Restricting to [-pi/2, pi/2] keeps every output from -1 to 1 exactly once, so that piece has an inverse.
stops.mistake: Thinking sin x already has an inverse without restricting it.
stops.again: If \(f\) has domain \([0, \pi]\) and range \([-1, 1]\), what are the domain and range of \(f^{-1}\)?
stops.againA: They swap: domain \([-1, 1]\), range \([0, \pi]\). These are the domain and range of \(\arccos\) when \(f\) is cosine restricted to \([0, \pi]\).
stops.reflect: Why do we have to restrict the domain of sine before it can have an inverse?

stages.desc: Evaluate each inverse within its allowed output range, then graph them and give the domain and range.

stops.title: Inverse sine
stops.target: \(\arcsin x\) is the angle in \(\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) whose sine is \(x\). Answers lie on the right half of the unit circle: in Quadrant I or Quadrant IV, or on an axis at \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(0\), or \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).
stops.coldA: \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), and \(-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\) (not \(\tfrac{5\pi}{4}\) or \(\tfrac{7\pi}{4}\), which are outside the range).
stops.solution: Which angle between -pi/2 and pi/2 has sine 1/2? pi/6. Which has sine -sqrt2/2? The negative value means Quadrant IV, written as a negative angle: -pi/4.
stops.mistake: Answering 7pi/4: it has the right sine but is outside [-pi/2, pi/2].
stops.reflect: Why are negative arcsin answers written as negative angles?
stops.stretch: Compute \(\arcsin(0)\) and \(\arcsin(1)\). Both answers are on an axis, in no quadrant.

stops.title: Inverse cosine
stops.target: \(\arccos x\) is the angle in \([0, \pi]\) whose cosine is \(x\). Answers lie on the top half of the unit circle: in Quadrant I or Quadrant II, or on an axis at \(0\), \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), or \(\pi\). They are never negative.
stops.coldA: \(\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\) (Quadrant II, since cosine is negative) and \(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\).
stops.solution: arccos(-sqrt3/2): the angle in [0, pi] with cosine -sqrt3/2. Negative cosine means Quadrant II, reference angle pi/6: pi - pi/6 = 5pi/6. arccos(sqrt2/2) = pi/4.
stops.mistake: Answering -pi/6 or -5pi/6 (arccos is never negative), or 7pi/6 (right cosine, but on the bottom half).
stops.reflect: Why is the range of arccos different from the range of arcsin?
stops.stretch: Compute \(\arccos(1)\). The answer is on an axis, in no quadrant.
stops.stretchA: \(0\), the right end of the top half.

stops.title: Inverse tangent
stops.target: \(\arctan x\) is the angle strictly between \(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) whose tangent is \(x\). Like arcsin, negative inputs give negative angles.
stops.solution: tan(pi/6) = (1/2)/(sqrt3/2) = 1/sqrt3 = sqrt3/3, so the angle strictly between -pi/2 and pi/2 with tangent -sqrt3/3 is -pi/6. tan(pi/4) = 1, so arctan(1) = pi/4.
stops.mistake: Answering 5pi/6 for arctan(-sqrt3/3): it has the right tangent but is outside (-pi/2, pi/2).
stops.reflect: Why are the endpoints \(\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}\) not included in the range of arctan?

stops.title: Extension: Inverse of a value outside the range
stops.target: Extension (beyond the PF3 CheckIt exercise, which shows the inside already evaluated): \(\arcsin(\sin(\theta))\) is not always \(\theta\). Evaluate the inside first, then find the angle in the inverse function's range.
stops.solution: Inside first: sin(5pi/6) = 1/2. Then arcsin(1/2) must be in [-pi/2, pi/2]: pi/6.
stops.mistake: Canceling arcsin and sin to get 5pi/6.

stops.title: Graph and state domain and range
stops.target: Graph each inverse from a table: swap the coordinates of the restricted sine, cosine, or tangent. arcsin: domain \([-1, 1]\), range \(\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\). arccos: domain \([-1, 1]\), range \([0, \pi]\). arctan: domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), range \(\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
stops.cold: Graph \(y = \arcsin x\). Give its domain and range.
stops.coldPlain: Graph y = arcsin x. Give its domain and range.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the endpoints or asymptotes, three key points, and the domain and range I found. Check my graph.
stops.solution: Take points of sin on [-pi/2, pi/2], like (-pi/2, -1), (-pi/6, -1/2), (0, 0), (pi/6, 1/2), (pi/2, 1), and swap them. The graph starts at (-1, -pi/2) and ends at (1, pi/2); it does not continue past x = plus or minus 1.
stops.mistake: Drawing the graph past x = 1 or x = -1.
stops.again: Graph \(y = \arccos x\) and \(y = \arctan x\). Give the domain and range of each.
stops.againA: arccos: domain \([-1, 1]\), range \([0, \pi]\). It falls from \((-1, \pi)\) to \((1, 0)\).[[graph:ACOS]]arctan: domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), range \(\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), with horizontal asymptotes at \(y = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}\).[[graph:ATAN]]
stops.reflect: Why does arctan have horizontal asymptotes, while tan had vertical ones?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the PF3 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Compute an inverse sine, cosine, and tangent, then give the domain and range of one inverse function and graph it.
stops.cold:
Part 1. Compute (a) \(\arcsin\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\) (b) \(\arccos(1)\) (c) \(\arctan\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\).

Part 2. Consider \(h(x) = \arccos x\). What are the domain and range of \(h\)? Draw a graph of \(h\).
stops.coldPlain: Part 1: Compute (a) arcsin(-sqrt3/2), (b) arccos(1), (c) arctan(-sqrt3/3). Part 2: For h(x) = arccos x, give the domain and range and draw the graph.
stops.note: I graphed it on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: the endpoints or asymptotes, three key points, and the domain and range I found. Check my graph.
stops.solution: (a) The angle in [-pi/2, pi/2] with sine -sqrt3/2 is -pi/3. (b) The angle in [0, pi] with cosine 1 is 0, the right end of the top half. (c) The angle strictly between -pi/2 and pi/2 with tangent -sqrt3/3 is -pi/6. Part 2: arccos takes inputs from -1 to 1 and outputs angles from 0 to pi.
stops.mistake: Giving answers outside each inverse function's range, like 5pi/3 for (a).
stops.again:
Part 1. Compute (a) \(\arcsin\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\) (b) \(\arccos\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\) (c) \(\arctan(\sqrt{3})\).

Part 2. Consider \(f(x) = \arctan x\). Give the domain and range and draw a graph.
stops.reflect: For each inverse, which half of the unit circle can the answer come from, and which axis angles are included?
